questions.question: What is the practical difference between declaring a permission in AndroidManifest.xml and the Info.plist usage-description string on iOS?
options: They are functionally identical with no real difference
The Info.plist string is actually shown to the user in the system permission dialog explaining why it's needed, while the manifest entry is just a build-time declaration
AndroidManifest.xml entries show a prompt to the user, Info.plist does not
Only Android requires any permission declaration at all
questions.explanation: iOS surfaces the Info.plist usage-description text directly to the user when requesting the permission; omitting it causes an instant crash rather than a silent failure.

questions.question: Why should you call `check()` before `request()` for a given permission?
options: check() is required syntax and has no functional purpose
Repeatedly calling request() after a user has already denied a permission can fail to re-prompt, since the OS often stops showing the dialog after a denial
request() always crashes if called twice
questions.explanation: Once a user denies a permission, the OS may stop presenting the native prompt again, so checking current status first lets the app decide whether to direct the user to Settings instead of re-requesting.

questions.question: What is the typical first step when a React Native app needs to access a device capability like the camera?
options: Always write a custom native module from scratch
Look for an existing, well-maintained community library before writing custom native code
Device APIs are not accessible from React Native at all
Request the permission before installing any library
questions.explanation: Common device APIs (camera, location, biometrics) almost always have existing, well-supported libraries — custom native modules are reserved for capabilities with no existing wrapper.

questions.question: When would writing a custom native module genuinely be necessary?
options: For any feature involving the camera
When integrating a native SDK or capability (e.g. a proprietary payment SDK) that has no existing React Native library wrapping it
Every React Native app requires at least one custom native module
Only when targeting Android, never iOS
questions.explanation: Custom native modules are for the narrower case where no community library already exposes the needed native functionality to JavaScript.
